title: Neuro-Ophthalmic Headaches: Clinical Scenarios & Management Masterclass
summary: An exhaustive clinical guide for identifying, triaging, and managing headaches in ophthalmic practice. From benign primary syndromes to life-threatening neuro-surgical emergencies, this poster covers 15 critical scenarios, workup protocols, and clinical pearls.

sections.title: The Neuro-Ophthalmic Headache Landscape
sections.content: Headache is one of the most common complaints in ophthalmic practice [32, 785]. While many cases are benign primary syndromes, the ophthalmologist must identify secondary causes that are life- or vision-threatening, such as Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA), intracranial mass lesions, and aneurysms [30, 567].

sections.title: Scenario 1: The Ophthalmic Emergency (GCA)
content: Scenario: 75-year-old female, 3-day history of severe right-sided temporal headache, malaise, and a 'shade' coming down over her vision for several minutes.
Diagnosis: Suspected Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) with amaurosis fugax [85, 760].
Red Flags: Scalp tenderness (pain when combing hair), jaw claudication (pain while chewing), and sudden visual loss [36, 85, 754].
Investigations: Immediate ESR, CRP, and Platelet count (Platelets are a strong predictor) [36, 757].
Gold standard: Temporal Artery Biopsy (TAB) (specimen >2 cm to avoid skip lesions) [5, 586, 762].
Management: Do not wait for biopsy results. Immediate IV Methylprednisolone (g/day for 3 days) followed by oral Prednisone ( mg/kg/day) [5, 89, 762].

sections.title: Scenario 2: The Obese Young Patient (IIH)
content: 1. Identify: 28-year-old obese female, constant global headache (worse in morning/coughing), 'greying out' (TVOs) when standing.
2. Clinical Picture: Papilledema (bilateral disc swelling), transient visual obscurations (TVOs), pulsatile tinnitus, and possible CN VI palsy [38, 40, 182].
3. Workup: Blood pressure check (exclude malignant HTN) [183]. Emergent MRI and MRV (rule out mass/venous thrombosis) [39, 183, 769].
4. LP: Lumbar puncture (LP) showing opening pressure ≥ 250 mm H2O with normal CSF composition [4, 184, 770].
5. Management: Weight loss primary [185, 554]. Acetazolamide (250 mg QID to g BID). Surgery: Optic nerve sheath fenestration (vision) or CSF shunting (headache) [44, 45, 554].

sections.title: Scenario 3: 'Worst Headache of My Life'
content: Scenario: 50-year-old male, sudden explosive headache, 'droopy' eyelid, double vision, large non-reactive pupil.
Diagnosis: Ruptured intracranial aneurysm (typically PCoA) causing Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH) [38, 199, 343].
Key Finding: Pupil-involving Third Nerve Palsy (fixed, dilated pupil) [0, 174, 198].
Action: Neurosurgical emergency. Urgent CTA preferred over MRA [202, 200, 346].
Treatment: Referral for endovascular coiling or surgical clipping [016, 346].

content.explanation: C: Conjunctival injection; L: Lacrimation; U: Unilateral (stabbing pain); S: Smoking history (35y male); T: Time-locked (2:00 AM); E: Eye/Ear autonomic signs (Rhinorrhea/Horner); R: Relief with 100% Oxygen (10–15 L/min) or Sumatriptan (6 mg SC). Prophylaxis: Verapamil or Lithium [157, 801, 1195].

sections.title: Scenario 5 & 6: Migraine & ICA Dissection
content: Scenario 5 (Migraine): 24-year-old female, 20-min shimmering zig-zag aura, followed by unilateral throbbing headache/nausea. Aura: 5–60 mins. Mgmt: Aspirin, Ibuprofen, Triptans. Avoid triggers [41, 795, 791].
Scenario 6 (ICA Dissection): 45-year-old male, acute temple/neck pain after car accident, small right pupil, 1 mm ptosis. Diagnosis: Internal Carotid Artery (ICA) Dissection [24, 180, 783].
Red Flag: A painful Horner syndrome is an ICA dissection until proven otherwise; high stroke risk. Mgmt: Urgent MRA/CTA head and neck; antiplatelet/anticoagulation [515, 784].

sections.title: Scenario 7 & 8: Pituitary & Trigeminal Pain
content: Scenario 7 (Pituitary Apoplexy): 40-year-old female, sudden severe headache, bilateral vision loss, total ophthalmoplegia. Red Flags: Bitemporal hemianopia, multiple CN palsies (III, IV, VI). Mgmt: Urgent MRI, immediate steroids to prevent Addisonian crisis [138, 802, 1532].

Scenario 8 (Trigeminal Neuralgia): 60-year-old male, 'electric shock-like' stabs in cheek triggered by shaving. Mgmt: Carbamazepine (100 mg BID up to 1200 mg/day) or Baclofen. Image to rule out MS or vascular compression [362, 805, 1197].

sections.title: Scenario 9: Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma
content: 1. Presentation: 65-year-old hyperope, sudden severe headache, eye pain, vomiting, hazy cornea.
2. Exam: IOP 50–80 mmHg, rock-hard eye, fixed mid-dilated vertically oval pupil, shallow anterior chamber [487, 681, 1235].
3. Acute Mgmt: Lie supine. Systemic Acetazolamide (500 mg IV) + topical suppressants.
4. Definitive: Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (PI) in BOTH eyes [488, 686, 1236].

sections.title: Scenario 10, 11, & 12: Inflammation, Meds, & Ischemia
content: Scenario 10 (Tolosa-Hunt): 50-year-old, intense boring orbital pain, CN III, IV, VI palsies. MRI shows apex enhancement. DX of exclusion (rule out lymphoma/aneurysm). Rx: Systemic steroids [962, 1800].
Scenario 11 (Medication Overuse): Chronic migraineur, headache ≥15 days/month, daily paracetamol/triptans. Mgmt: Abruptly stop offending drug (withdrawal lasts ~3 weeks) [838, 1012].

Scenario 12 (Ocular Ischemic Syndrome): 70-year-old, carotid disease, dull aching 'ocular angina', vision improves in dark. Mid-peripheral dot-blot hemorrhages, iris neovascularization. Mgmt: Carotid endarterectomy; manage IOP/PRP [81, 1597].

sections.title: Scenario 13, 14, & 15: Tension, Meningitis, & Raeder
content: Scenario 13 (Tension): 30-year-old student, 'viselike' band, worse end of day. Bilateral, pressing, no physical aggravation. Rx: NSAIDs, Amitriptyline [153, 798].

Scenario 14 (Meningitis): 20-year-old, severe headache, neck stiffness, photophobia. Pearl: Pain on eye movement is common; normal ocular exam. Mgmt: LP (after CT if focal) + IV antibiotics [139, 1568].
Scenario 15 (Raeder Paratrigeminal): Middle-aged man, Horner syndrome + daily unilateral periorbital headaches (V1). Mgmt: Exclude parasellar/cavernous sinus pathology with MRI [126, 807].

branches: Life-Threatening Screening: Sudden (Aneurysm), Fever (Meningitis), Age >55 (GCA), High BP (Crisis)
Detailed History: Timing (Morning=ICP, Night=Cluster), Triggers (Touch=CN V, Food=Migraine)
Special Tests: Hertel (Proptosis), Corneal Sensation (CN V), LP (if imaging normal)
Labs: ESR/CRP/FBC for all patients >50 years

sections.title: Comprehensive Ocular Examination
content: Pupils: Check for RAPD (Optic nerve) and Anisocoria (Horner/CN III).
Fundus: Look for Disc edema (Papilledema/GCA) and Hemorrhages (HTN/CRVO).
IOP/Gonio: Crucial to exclude Acute Glaucoma.
Motility: Identify CN III, IV, or VI palsies indicating compressive lesions.

content.explanation: Pearl: SVP absence is common in papilledema, but presence strongly suggests normal ICP [1572]. Pitfall: Never LP before neuroimaging if mass suspected (herniation risk). Examiner's Pick: Headache + Adie-like pupil? Check for CN III aberrant regeneration. Precaution: Beta-blockers for glaucoma can mask migraine/systemic signs. High Yield: Pregnant + Headache + Vision Loss? Consider Preeclampsia/Eclampsia & PRES.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis: The SNOOP Mnemonic
content: S: Systemic signs/symptoms (Fever, Weight Loss, Pregnancy)
N: Neurologic signs (Palsies, Papilledema, RAPD)
O: Onset (Sudden, Thunderbolt, Explosive)
O: Older age of onset (>50 years, GCA risk)
P: Progression or Pattern change (New type of headache)

Headache in Neuro-Ophthalmology: Clinical Scenarios & Management
Headache is one of the most common complaints in ophthalmic practice [32, 785]. While many cases are benign primary syndromes, the ophthalmologist must identify secondary causes that are life- or vision-threatening, such as Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA), intracranial mass lesions, and aneurysms [30, 567].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
OSCE & VIVA Clinical Scenarios
Scenario 1: The Ophthalmic Emergency (GCA)
Scenario: A 75-year-old female presents with a 3-day history of severe right-sided temporal headache, malaise, and a "shade" coming down over her vision for several minutes.
Diagnosis: Suspected Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) with amaurosis fugax [85, 760].
Red Flags: Scalp tenderness (pain when combing hair), jaw claudication (pain while chewing), and sudden visual loss [36, 85, 754].
Investigations: Immediate ESR, CRP, and Platelet count (Platelets are a strong predictor) [36, 757]. Gold standard: Temporal Artery Biopsy (TAB) (specimen >2 cm to avoid skip lesions) [5, 586, 762].
Management: Do not wait for biopsy results. Immediate IV Methylprednisolone (g/day for 3 days) followed by oral Prednisone ( mg/kg/day) [5, 89, 762].
Scenario 2: The Obese Young Patient (IIH)
Scenario: A 28-year-old obese female reports a constant global headache that is worse in the morning and intensified by coughing. She describes brief "greying out" of vision when standing up.
Diagnosis: Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH) [37, 83, 768].
Clinical Picture: Papilledema (bilateral disc swelling), transient visual obscurations (TVOs), pulsatile tinnitus, and possible CN VI palsy [38, 40, 82].
Workup: Blood pressure check (exclude malignant HTN) [83]. Emergent MRI and MRV to rule out mass lesions or venous sinus thrombosis [39, 83, 769]. Lumbar puncture (LP) showing opening pressure ≥ 250 mm H 
2
​	
 O with normal CSF composition [4, 84, 770].
Management: Weight loss is primary [85, 554]. Acetazolamide (250 mg QID building to g BID) [554]. Surgical options: Optic nerve sheath fenestration (vision threat) or CSF shunting (headache threat) [44, 45, 554].
Scenario 3: "Worst Headache of My Life" (Aneurysm/SAH)
Scenario: A 50-year-old male presents with a sudden, explosive headache and a "droopy" right eyelid. On lifting the lid, he has double vision and the right pupil is large and non-reactive.
Diagnosis: Ruptured intracranial aneurysm (typically Posterior Communicating Artery [PCoA]) causing Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH) [38, 99, 343].
Key Finding: Pupil-involving Third Nerve Palsy (fixed, dilated pupil) [0, 74, 98].
Threat: Neurosurgical emergency [38, 99].
Management: Urgent CTA or MRA (CTA is preferred for acuity) [202, 200, 346]. Referral to neurosurgery for endovascular coiling or surgical clipping [06, 346].
Scenario 4: The "Suicide" Headache (Cluster Headache)
Scenario: A 35-year-old male smoker reports excruciating, stabbing pain behind his left eye occurring every night at 2:00 AM for the last two weeks. The eye is red and tearing.
Diagnosis: Cluster Headache [57, 80, 95].
Signs: Ipsilateral conjunctival injection, lacrimation, rhinorrhea, and miosis/ptosis (Horner syndrome) [58, 803, 95].
Management: Acute: 00% Oxygen (0–5 L/min for 5 mins) and Sumatriptan (6 mg SC) [803, 582]. Prophylaxis: Verapamil or Lithium [583].
Scenario 5: Classic Migraine with Aura
Scenario: A 24-year-old female experiences shimmering zig-zag lights in her vision for 20 minutes, followed by a throbbing unilateral headache with nausea.
Diagnosis: Migraine with typical aura [4, 795, 79].
Key Points: Aura usually lasts 5–60 minutes and is followed by headache within 60 minutes [42, 796, 79].
Management: Acute: Aspirin, Ibuprofen, or Triptans (e.g., Sumatriptan 50–00 mg PO) [55, 797, 582]. Avoid triggers like caffeine withdrawal, stress, and specific foods [54, 797, 576].
Scenario 6: Painful Horner Syndrome (ICA Dissection)
Scenario: A 45-year-old male has acute pain in the right temple and neck after a minor car accident. He is noted to have a small right pupil and  mm of ptosis.
Diagnosis: Internal Carotid Artery (ICA) Dissection [24, 80, 783].
Highlight: A painful Horner syndrome is an ICA dissection until proven otherwise; it carries a high risk of stroke [24, 202, 783].
Management: Urgent MRA or CTA of the head and neck [20, 80, 54]. Antiplatelet or anticoagulation therapy [55, 784].
Scenario 7: Pituitary Apoplexy
Scenario: A 40-year-old female presents with a sudden severe headache, bilateral vision loss, and total ophthalmoplegia.
Diagnosis: Pituitary Apoplexy [38, 802, 532].
Mechanism: Infarction or hemorrhage of a pituitary adenoma [38, 532].
Red Flags: Bitemporal hemianopia or blindness, sudden multiple CN palsies (III, IV, VI) [38, 802, 8].
Management: Urgent MRI. Immediate corticosteroid replacement to prevent life-threatening Addisonian crisis [802, 754].
Scenario 8: Trigeminal Neuralgia
Scenario: A 60-year-old male describes "electric shock-like" stabs of pain in his right cheek triggered by shaving or light touch.
Diagnosis: Trigeminal Neuralgia (Tic Douloureux) [362, 805, 97].
Management: Carbamazepine (00 mg BID, increasing up to 200 mg/day) or Baclofen [03, 96, 97]. Neuroimaging to exclude vascular compression or MS [3, 76].
Scenario 9: Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma
Scenario: A 65-year-old hyperopic female presents with sudden severe headache, eye pain, and vomiting. The eye is rock-hard and the cornea is hazy.
Diagnosis: Acute Primary Angle Closure (APAC) [487, 68, 235].
Examination Pick: High IOP (50–80 mmHg), fixed mid-dilated vertically oval pupil, and shallow anterior chamber [487, 68, 235].
Management: Lie supine. Systemic Acetazolamide (500 mg IV) and topical suppressants [685, 899, 478]. Definitive: Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (PI) in both eyes [488, 686, 236].
Scenario 10: Tolosa-Hunt Syndrome
Scenario: A 50-year-old presents with intense boring orbital pain and multiple ocular motor nerve palsies (III, IV, VI). MRI shows enhancement at the orbital apex.
Diagnosis: Tolosa-Hunt Syndrome (idiopathic granulomatous inflammation) [249, 96, 533, 800].
Examiner's Pick: Diagnosis of exclusion; must rule out lymphoma, metastasis, and aneurysm [, 96, 458].
Management: Highly responsive to systemic steroids (Prednisone  mg/kg/day) [962, 458, 800].
Scenario 11: Medication Overuse Headache
Scenario: A chronic migraineur reports a headache on ≥ 5 days per month for the last four months. She is taking paracetamol and triptans daily.
Diagnosis: Medication Overuse Headache [838, 02].
Management: Counsel patient to abruptly stop the offending drug (withdrawal may last 3 weeks) [800, 02].
Scenario 12: Ocular Ischemic Syndrome (OIS)
Scenario: A 70-year-old male with known carotid disease presents with a dull, aching periorbital headache ("ocular angina") and blurred vision that improves in the dark.
Diagnosis: Ocular Ischemic Syndrome [8, 293, 597].
Clinical Picture: Mid-peripheral dot-and-blot hemorrhages, dilated (nontortuous) veins, and iris neovascularization [8, 708].
Management: Carotid endarterectomy; manage IOP and retinal ischemia (PRP) [82, 600].
Scenario 13: Tension-Type Headache
Scenario: A 30-year-old law student describes a "viselike" band of pain around her head, typically worse at the end of a long day of studying.
Diagnosis: Tension-type headache [53, 798].
Key Points: Bilateral, pressing quality, not aggravated by physical activity.
Management: Simple analgesics (NSAIDs); prophylactic tricyclic antidepressants (Amitriptyline) [55, 799].
Scenario 14: Meningitis masquerading as Ocular Pain
Scenario: A 20-year-old presents with a severe headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia.
Diagnosis: Meningitis [39, 350, 568].
Clinical Pearl: Pain on eye movement and photophobia are common; normal ocular exam [39, 568].
Management: Immediate LP (after CT if focal signs present) and IV antibiotics [64, 55].
Scenario 15: Raeder Paratrigeminal Syndrome
Scenario: A middle-aged man presents with Horner syndrome and daily unilateral periorbital headaches in the V1 distribution.
Diagnosis: Raeder Syndrome [26, 807, 80].
Management: Must exclude intracranial pathology in the parasellar or cavernous sinus regions with MRI [26, 807, 80].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Comparisons: Primary vs. Secondary Headaches
Feature
Primary (Migraine/Cluster/Tension)
Secondary (GCA/IIH/Aneurysm)
Onset
Often chronic/recurrent [40]
Can be sudden/new [3, 566]
Systemic Symptoms
Rare (except nausea) [4, 792]
Fever, weight loss, jaw pain [36, 85]
Neurological Signs
Transient aura only [42, 008]
Persistent palsies, disc edema [37, 82]
Urgency
Non-urgent treatment [54]
Immediate medical/surgical referral [30, 99]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Workup & Approach Mind Map
Life-Threatening Screening (Triage):
Sudden "Worst" headache? → Aneurysm/SAH [38].
Fever + Stiff neck? → Meningitis [39].
Age >55 + Scalp tenderness? → GCA [36].
Malignant BP? → Hypertensive Crisis [568].
Detailed History:
Timing: Morning (High ICP), Evening (Tension), Night (Cluster) [37, 53, 58].
Triggers: Touch (Trigeminal Neuralgia), Alcohol (Cluster), Foods (Migraine) [58, 03, 576].
Comprehensive Ocular Exam:
Pupils: RAPD (Optic nerve lesion), Anisocoria (Horner/CN III) [8, 22, 98].
Fundus: Disc edema (Papilledema/GCA), Hemorrhages (HTN/CRVO) [82, 548, 585].
IOP/Gonio: Exclude Acute Glaucoma [235, 475].
Special Tests:
Hertel Exophthalmometry (Proptosis) [429, 439].
Corneal Sensation (Exclude CN V involvement) [, 300].
Imaging & Labs:
ESR/CRP/FBC for all >50 years [79, 762].
MRI/MRV (Soft tissue/Sinuses) vs. CT/CTA (Bone/Blood/Vessels).
Lumbar Puncture (If imaging normal and ICP suspected) [37, 83].
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Management Highlights: Pearls & Pitfalls
Pearl: The absence of Spontaneous Venous Pulsations (SVPs) is common in papilledema, but its presence strongly suggests normal ICP [572].
Pitfall: Do not perform an LP before neuroimaging if a mass lesion is suspected, as this can lead to brainstem herniation [64, 83].
Examiner's Pick: In a patient with headache and an "Adie-like" pupil, always check for aberrant regeneration of CN III, which could indicate an old compressive lesion [9, 74].
Precaution: Topical Beta-blockers for glaucoma can worsen migraine management or mask systemic signs [892, 53].
High Yield: In pregnant women with headaches and visual loss, always consider Preeclampsia/Eclampsia and Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome (PRES) [403, 779, 9].
